passage: Sunday diary. Today in the Arts Hall Mr. Farooq talked about volcanoes, and his voice never went up or down, like a fan. I nearly fell asleep. Salma whispered, “He doesn't care.” But then I saw that he had dark circles and kept drinking water. Maybe he was very tired. Salma herself talks in a flat way when she is shy, and she cares a lot about everything. Then I remembered my cousin, who speaks in that flat voice all the time, and he loves his class and explains stuff beautifully. So a flat voice doesn't mean someone doesn't care. Kiran.

qa.q: What was Mr. Farooq talking about?
qa.a: Volcanoes.

qa.q: What did Kiran think about Mr. Farooq's flat voice, and what did Kiran notice?
qa.a: Kiran first felt sleepy and bored, but then noticed Mr. Farooq's dark circles and thought he might be tired, so stopped assuming he did not care.

qa.q: What could Kiran do if Kiran wants to understand a friend with a flat voice?
qa.a: Kiran could ask about the topic or watch what the friend does, not judge by tone alone.

qa.q: How might Salma have seen Mr. Farooq's voice?
qa.a: Salma took it as not caring, though Kiran suggests that could be wrong.

grounding: A pupil hears a flat, monotone voice and learns it may show tiredness, shyness or a speaking style, not a lack of caring.

passage: In the village school under the neem tree, Hansa's new teacher spoke in an even, soft voice and never smiled much. At first the children were unsure. Arohi whispered to Hansa, “She sounds cross.” Hansa shook her head. “She gave me her own pencil yesterday.” Later the teacher walked past every child's slate and quietly praised each drawing. When Arohi got hers praised, she looked shocked, then pleased. “Her voice is just like that,” Hansa said. “Maybe her voice is calm, or maybe she's tired. She isn't cross.” Arohi nodded and took her slate back to her seat.

qa.q: Where was the school?
qa.a: In a village, under a neem tree.

qa.q: Why did Hansa think the teacher was not cross, despite her flat voice?
qa.a: Hansa remembered the teacher giving her a pencil and saw her praising every drawing, so she trusted the actions more than the tone.

qa.q: What could Arohi try next time a teacher's voice makes her nervous?
qa.a: She could look at what the teacher does, like sharing pencils and praising drawings, and ask a question if she is still unsure.

qa.q: How might the teacher feel if children read her voice as cross?
qa.a: She might feel misunderstood, since her even voice is just how she speaks and she cares about her pupils.

grounding: A flat, even voice from a teacher is not proof of not caring, and the children learn to read actions along with tone.

passage: When Valentina gave Sofia the bracelet she'd made, Sofia looked at it and said, in her usual flat voice, “Thanks. It's nice.” No squeal, no smile. Valentina's heart sank all the way home through the Buenos Aires traffic. She doesn't like it. The next morning, Sofia was wearing the bracelet. She wore it the next day, and the next. At lunch, in the same level voice, she said, “I wear it every day. I don't even take it off to shower.” Valentina laughed. Sofia's mother had once told her, “Sofia's voice stays flat even when she's very happy. Watch what she does.” Now Valentina understood.

qa.q: What did Valentina give Sofia?
qa.a: Valentina gave Sofia a bracelet she had made.

qa.q: What was Valentina feeling on the way home?
qa.a: Valentina felt disappointed and hurt, thinking Sofia's flat thanks meant she didn't like the bracelet.

qa.q: What helped Valentina read Sofia correctly?
qa.a: Watching what Sofia did, wearing the bracelet every day, and remembering her mother's words that her voice stays flat even when happy.

qa.q: How might Sofia feel if people often read her flat voice as not caring?
qa.a: Sofia might feel misunderstood and frustrated, since she cares a lot but her voice doesn't show it.

grounding: Shows a friend's flat voice being her personal speaking style, not a sign that she doesn't care.

passage: By the last period, Aparna Ma'am's voice had gone flat and even, like a ruler. When Pooja showed her the model of the solar system she had worked on all week, Ma'am said, “Good. Put it on the shelf,” without any rise or fall. Pooja's smile slipped. She hates it. Back at her desk, she almost pulled Saturn off. Then she noticed Ma'am rubbing her temples and sipping water, and the pile of copies still to check. At the end of class Pooja asked, “Ma'am, was it really okay?” Aparna Ma'am looked up, and her voice warmed a little. “It's lovely. I'm just very tired. Sorry, Pooja.”

qa.q: What had Pooja made?
qa.a: Pooja had made a model of the solar system.

qa.q: What was Pooja feeling when Ma'am spoke in a flat voice?
qa.a: Pooja felt hurt and discouraged, thinking Ma'am didn't care about the model she had worked on all week.

qa.q: What did Pooja notice that changed her reading?
qa.a: She noticed Ma'am rubbing her temples, sipping water and the pile of copies, which suggested tiredness, so she asked instead of assuming.

qa.q: What was the last period like for Aparna Ma'am?
qa.a: Aparna Ma'am was exhausted after a long day, and her flat voice came from tiredness, not a lack of care.

grounding: Shows a pupil hearing a tired teacher's flat voice as not caring, and noticing tiredness before judging.

passage: I'm Wasim. When our new classmate Pankaj stood up to introduce himself, he said, in a completely flat voice, “I'm Pankaj. I like chess. I moved from Nagpur.” No smile, no up and down. Somebody behind me whispered, “He sounds like he doesn't want to be here.” I wasn't sure. But I saw his hands. He was holding his shirt hem so tight his knuckles were white, and he sat down the moment he finished. At break I asked if he wanted a game. In the same flat voice he said, “Yes. I would like that very much.” He beat me in eleven moves.

qa.q: Where did Pankaj move from?
qa.a: Pankaj moved from Nagpur.

qa.q: What might Pankaj have been feeling during his introduction?
qa.a: He was probably shy and nervous, gripping his shirt hem tightly; his flat voice may also simply be his usual way of speaking.

qa.q: What did Wasim do that the whisperer didn't?
qa.a: Wasim looked for other clues, like the tight grip, and then invited Pankaj to play, instead of deciding he didn't care.

qa.q: How did the whisperer read Pankaj's voice?
qa.a: The whisperer read the flat voice as not wanting to be there, missing the nerves behind it.

grounding: Shows a shy new classmate's flat, monotone voice being misread as not caring, when it came from nerves or personal style.

passage:
Monday: Kashish burst into class. "I got into the state chess team!" Mehak looked up. "That's nice," she said, flat as a table. Kashish's smile slid off. She doesn't even care.

Wednesday: In art, Mehak spent the whole hour drawing her dog, Biscuit, down to every whisker. "He is my favourite being in the world," she told Kashish, in the same flat, even voice. Kashish frowned. That didn't sound like not caring. It sounded like just… Mehak.

Friday: "Can I ask something? When I told you about chess, did you mind?" Mehak blinked. "Mind? I was so happy for you. My voice just comes out like that. Mum says I sound like the radio weather." Kashish laughed.

qa.q: What did Mehak draw in art on Wednesday?
qa.a: Her dog, Biscuit, down to every whisker.

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling when Mehak said "That's nice" so flatly on Monday?
qa.a: Hurt and let down, thinking Mehak didn't care about the big news, as her sliding smile shows.

qa.q: What helped Kashish understand Mehak's voice?
qa.a: Noticing that Mehak used the same flat voice for something she clearly loved, and then simply asking on Friday.

qa.q: What is it like for Mehak to have her flat voice misread?
qa.a: Mehak was truly happy for Kashish, so being read as uncaring can leave her misunderstood without even knowing it.

grounding: It shows a child misreading a friend's flat, even voice as not caring, then learning it is simply her speaking style.
